scenes.tts: An axon grows toward the midline of the nervous system. It crosses. Then it treats that same midline as forbidden ground. What changed?
scenes.visual: Title card. Transverse section of a spinal cord, dorsal up. One axon grows down to the ventral midline, crosses, and continues on the far side. Question on screen: what changed?
scenes.narration: An axon grows toward the midline of the nervous system. It crosses. Then it treats that same midline as forbidden ground. What changed?

scenes.tts: Your left and right sides have to talk. Much touch and pain information from one side ends up in the opposite half of the brain.
scenes.visual: A body outline with a touch on the left hand; a line runs up and crosses to the right half of the brain.
scenes.narration: Your left and right sides have to talk. Much touch and pain information from one side ends up in the opposite half of the brain.

scenes.tts: The two halves of the spinal cord also coordinate walking. Both jobs need commissural axons, axons that cross the midline.
scenes.visual: Two legs stepping in alternation, linked by axons crossing the spinal cord. Label: commissural axons.
scenes.narration: The two halves of the spinal cord also coordinate walking. Both jobs need commissural axons, axons that cross the midline.

scenes.tts: Their neighbours, ipsilateral axons, stay on the side where they started. They must never cross.
scenes.visual: Back to the cord section: a second axon beside the first runs along its own side and never reaches the midline. Label: ipsilateral axon.
scenes.narration: Their neighbours, ipsilateral axons, stay on the side where they started. They must never cross.

scenes.tts: A commissural axon has three jobs. Grow toward the midline. Enter it and leave it. And never come back.
scenes.visual: Three numbered tags appear along the commissural axon's path: 1 approach, 2 cross and leave, 3 never return.
scenes.narration: A commissural axon has three jobs. Grow toward the midline. Enter it and leave it. And never come back.

scenes.tts: Each job fails in a different way. If the pull still beats the push after crossing, the axon stalls there.
scenes.visual: Ghost axon 1: reaches the floor plate and stops inside it, a pull arrow still stronger than a push arrow. Label: stall.
scenes.narration: Each job fails in a different way. If the pull still beats the push after crossing, the axon stalls there.

scenes.tts: Get repelled too early, and it never crosses at all. Lose the repulsion after crossing, and it might wander back.
scenes.visual: Ghost axon 2 turns away before the midline (never crosses). Ghost axon 3 crosses, then loops back across (recross).
scenes.narration: Get repelled too early, and it never crosses at all. Lose the repulsion after crossing, and it might wander back.

scenes.tts: Now look at the midline itself. In the fly it is a row of glial cells. In the spinal cord it is the floor plate.
scenes.visual: Split screen: fly nerve cord midline glia on the left, vertebrate floor plate on the right, both highlighted.
scenes.narration: Now look at the midline itself. In the fly it is a row of glial cells. In the spinal cord it is the floor plate.

scenes.tts: The same cells present the same molecules before, during and after an axon passes. The midline did not change.
scenes.visual: Three snapshots of the same floor plate as an axon approaches, crosses and leaves; the floor plate is identical in all three. Label: same cells, same molecules.
scenes.narration: The same cells present the same molecules before, during and after an axon passes. The midline did not change.

scenes.tts: So the change has to be in the axon.
scenes.visual: The camera zooms to the growth cone. Label: the change is here.
scenes.narration: So the change has to be in the axon.

scenes.tts: That leaves three puzzles. Why does an axon drawn to the midline leave it? Why does it never come back? And why do its ipsilateral neighbours never cross at all?
scenes.visual: Three numbered puzzle cards appear on screen, one per question.
scenes.narration: That leaves three puzzles. Why does an axon drawn to the midline leave it? Why does it never come back? And why do its ipsilateral neighbours never cross at all?

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea to carry through. While an axon crosses, the midline stays the same. The axon changes what it can hear.
scenes.visual: Rule card: While an axon crosses, the midline stays the same; the axon changes what it can hear.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea to carry through. While an axon crosses, the midline stays the same. The axon changes what it can hear.

scenes.tts: The midline makes a repellent called Slit. The growth cone carries Robo receptors that hear it.
scenes.visual: Slit dots spread from the floor plate. Robo receptors drawn as small ears on the growth cone membrane.
scenes.narration: The midline makes a repellent called Slit. The growth cone carries Robo receptors that hear it.

scenes.tts: In a simple toy model, the axon's push is Slit times the repelling Robo activity on its growth cone.
scenes.visual: On screen: push ≈ Slit × Robo activity. Small label: toy model.
scenes.narration: In a simple toy model, the axon's push is Slit times the repelling Robo activity on its growth cone.

scenes.tts: The axon is turned away only when that push passes a threshold.
scenes.visual: An illustrative S-shaped curve: push on the x axis, chance of being turned away on the y axis; a dashed threshold line. Label: toy model.
scenes.narration: The axon is turned away only when that push passes a threshold.

scenes.tts: Ipsilateral axons keep the push high from the start. Commissural axons hold it low until they have crossed. Then they let it rise.
scenes.visual: Two push meters ride along the two axons: the ipsilateral meter is high throughout; the commissural meter is low until the far side, then rises past the threshold.
scenes.narration: Ipsilateral axons keep the push high from the start. Commissural axons hold it low until they have crossed. Then they let it rise.

scenes.tts: Flies do this with a protein called Comm. Mammals do it with a relative of Robo, called Robo three.
scenes.caption: Flies do this with a protein called Comm. Mammals do it with a relative of Robo, called Robo3.
scenes.visual: Two labels under the commissural meter: flies, Comm; mammals, Robo3.
scenes.narration: Flies do this with a protein called Comm. Mammals do it with a relative of Robo, called Robo3.

scenes.tts: So a Slit and Robo mutant can be read with three questions. Is Slit there? Can the axon hear it? When does it start hearing it?
scenes.visual: The three questions on screen, stacked: Is Slit there? Can the axon hear it? When does it start hearing it?
scenes.narration: So a Slit and Robo mutant can be read with three questions. Is Slit there? Can the axon hear it? When does it start hearing it?

scenes.tts: The takeaway: the midline stays the same, and the axon changes what it can hear, and when. That is the repulsion side of the story.
scenes.visual: The cord section again, with the commissural axon across and its push meter high. Rule card returns, with a small note: repulsion only.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: the midline stays the same, and the axon changes what it can hear, and when. That is the repulsion side of the story.
